utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we start, there's a matter I would like to announce, that is this case will make a break on the 25th of May for -- of -- 25th of April until the 11th of May. That is about two weeks and a half. This Bench understands that there are some motions filed from both parties. I hope that the parties would file their reply as early as possible. If they file any response in the two weeks' time, this Bench will be in break. So I hope that the parties could file their response, if there's any, as early as possible. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we will do so, and as early as possible means it may be this week to the one that -- we've received one and we think we can respond fairly quickly to that one. Can I just foreshadow that there -- Your Honours, you inquired of both parties concerning our -- effectively asking for some assistance from the parties concerning what should happen with the witness Karic, or with the deposition of Mr. Karic. And I was rather acutely aware that on some matters we were - at least the Defence, I won't speak for the Prosecutor, but certainly the Defence - we were of less assistance that I would like to have been on some matters. What I have in mind is that I've drafted a motion in support of what was put in argument. It shouldn't be -- it shouldn't really expand the terms of things, but I just felt frankly I didn't -- it might not be a question of doing a good job, I didn't put everything that could assist the Tribunal. As soon as that's done, we'll forward that to the Tribunal I think in order to preserve formal continuity we'll just file it as a motion in the normal way, but when the Tribunal receives it will be in the context that you have already heard some argument. It has been cut down. So therefore, it is by way of supplementary argument and perhaps a little more complete in some respects. What it addresses is a number of issues, and the Prosecution will be given a copy as soon as it's filed, but just so they know what is coming and have time to respond as best they can. It deals with a number of scenarios, because Your Honours may make a decision that there should be no further cross-examination. If that's the case, that's the end of the arguments, really. If you say there should be allowed some further cross-examination, other possibilities arise, what topics we can cross-examine on. If so, the Prosecution have asked that they should be allowed to ask some questions on new topics as well as. What I've sought to be is organise the argument dealing with hypotheticals. Frankly, I know that some of them are hypothetical and you may or may not get to those. You may rule against us getting leave to further cross-examine at all and we understand that. That's why it's set out in a way that allows what I hope -- orderly decision-making and orderly argument, and that's why I will provide that extra material. Can I just say I apologise that we didn't have that at the time. Your Honours asked for us an oral argument and I would have liked to have done something more complete and better than I did, frankly. We were busy at the time. So that's why it happened the way it did. That will be filed within the next two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information and this Bench will regard this filing as supplementary material rather than a new filing. Whether the Prosecution would like to respond, that is their discretion. I believe that it depends on whether there are some new elements involved in that supplementary materials, because we already had our oral argument in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. Could I indicate there's one matter that I've addressed which was mentioned but I don't think explored in argument to any great degree in the oral submissions, and that is the question of what should happen to any materials that were sought to be tendered during the course of that deposition. You may recall that there was at one stage an attempt to put the whole statement of is to him and I'm not sure what the Prosecution's intentions are about that, but I'll put our intentions on the map anyway in the draft that I have. The Prosecution will have the opportunity to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest during the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It won't be long for today, I promise you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Morrissey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness G. When we stopped last week I had finished asking you some questions about that short glance you took at document on the desk of Commander Buza and I wanted to move on to the events of the 13th of September. You have indicated to the Tribunal that on the 13th of September you and the rest of the soldiers were effectively waiting to go into battle. And my question is: Were you waiting at Dobro Polje or were you waiting in that assembly area which you indicated on a photograph behind the village of Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were waiting at Dobro Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And were the -- were the soldiers also waiting at Dobro Polje or was it just people who had some official function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were also waiting. They were ready to be committed. We were all waiting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Very well. Now, the soldiers and I suppose the officers as well were all -- had already been told that they were to go into battle at some stage on the 13th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated last Friday [sic] that you were not present when Sefer Halilovic addressed the troops on the 13th -- sorry. Pardon me. I take that back. On the 12th of September, but you heard about that from the officer in charge of personnel matters. Could I just ask you: Do you remember the name of that officer in charge of personnel matters who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Sead Colak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And Colak is -- yes, thank you. I see it's spelled correctly on the screen. All right. Now, moving to -- moving back to the day, the 13th of September. At what time did you expect you were going into battle? I understand that in fact you didn't go into battle, but at what time did you think you were going to go into battle that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to go into battle on the morning of the 13th, early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Early morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- the same time as all the other units in our northern sector, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Did Buza -- did Enver Buza provide any explanation to you before Sefer Halilovic arrived as to why you were not going into battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never provided any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Did he have in his employment in the battalion at that time an individual called Erzimana Dogic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was a lady who worked with him. She was dealing with intelligence-relating mattered. Her name was Erzimana Dogic, and she was a much-trusted colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, are you able to recall the approximate time at which Sefer Halilovic arrived on the 13th after your unit had not gone into battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically what time it was. I don't think it could have been before noon, though. It may have been sometime in the early afternoon once it had become clear that we were not going to go into battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether you came from the direction of Voljevac or whether he was heading towards Voljevac when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain where he had come from, but he may have come from the direction of Voljevac. But I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are you able to draw a conclusion about that question from the direction in which his car drove off after he spoke to Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question with any degree of certainty. I seem to remember that he drove off to Jablanica, but I can't be sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to Sefer Halilovic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I had had a chance to speak to him, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you indicated that his speech to the troops on this occasion was a short one. Is it accurate to say that it lasted five minutes or less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even five minutes. He only said several sentences; that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. And in total, how long did he seem to spend at Dobro Polje on that occasion? Was it 15 minutes or half an hour or an hour, doing the best you can to estimate how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of these events is limited and therefore I can't be very precise in my answer. However, on the 13th I don't think he could possibly have stayed longer than 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, sometime after Sefer left the troops received a speech from their own commander, Enver Buza. Now, I wanted to ask you this: Had Buza ever made a speech like that -- well, perhaps I should ask you -- first of all, I'll ask you about the speech itself. You indicated he was very animated and emotional during that speech. Had you ever seen him make an animated, emotional speech before that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said his speech had been emotional, but he did not seem shaken. It was an emotional speech; he yelled a lot, that sort of thing. I wish I could remember the actual things he said but I can't. I remember the expression on his face. I remember the fact that he was yelling and making a lot of noise. He seldom spoke like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I was going to say -- well, that really was my question. Had he ever spoken like that when addressing the troops before a combat operation in your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he seldom spoke like that. I do remember him addressing people in that way a couple of times, though. Once he spoke to the local population, civilian population, of a village in much the same manner. So that must more or less have been his style of addressing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now I want to move to the action itself, the fighting. And I just have a couple of photographs I want you to mark. I understand you've already done a number of these, but there's two I'd like you to deal with very quickly, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: First of all, could the witness be shown P335, P335.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a panoramic shot from the village of Cer. Last week you marked a photograph with artillery positions, and this particular photograph -- this particular photograph may allow you to mark some further artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So could the witness please be given the marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just using a small blue circle, as you have in the past, could you just mark in whereabouts in that photograph one can see HVO artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction, if I may. This isn't Cer; this is Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the view opens towards HVO-controlled territory. What I can mark for you here is the artillery positions that were in the area of Kranjcici village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you just mark Kranjcici above that circle. And while you're doing that, can you accept my apologies. I don't know why I said Cer. We've been through the village of Here quite a number of times so I apologise for that and thanks for correcting it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Those are artillery positions at Kranjcici. Could you just sort of explain to the Tribunal what sort of guns did they have up on Kranjcici. Was there an anti-aircraft gun there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually there was a tank. There were two or several mortars, we weren't sure, and there was a multiple rocket launcher too in this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an anti-aircraft gun here, at this location called Gradac. Do you want me to mark that for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Please do and mark "Gradac" beside that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And underneath the word "Gradac" would you mark "AA" to indicate anti-aircraft.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are there any other HVO artillery positions that can be seen or the location of which can be seen in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were artillery positions near the school building around here. It's called Cer. Furthermore, there were lower-calibre mortars, 60-millimetre mortars, around here, too, on top of the hill. The hill's name is Borak. The village of Here was within the range of the artillery that was positioned at Prozor, but you can't see it in this photograph. Just to the left from the area that the photograph shows, there's an elevation with a tank and a number of other artillery pieces that were being used to fire both on Here and other positions and villages that at the time were under the control of the BH army. Just to the left of the area the photograph shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you write next to the circle at Cer the word "Cer" and then write "Borak" next to the position of Borak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you draw an arrow on the picture pointing in the direction of where the Prozor artillery was, which can't be seen in this current photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] This place was also within the range of other artillery positions. We weren't sure where those positions were. There was no way for us to know their precise whereabouts, but it was probably further south of Prozor in the village of Lug. It might have been in this general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, before I tender that document, I just want to ask you some questions about the practices of those guns, those artillery guns, that are on those positions. In the weeks before the fighting in Uzdol on the 14th of September, did those guns fire upon the village of Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with certainty that from the 24th of October, 1992 until the date you've referred to they fired on countless times. The village had been destroyed by artillery times by the time we are now considering. The army BH was entirely inferior as far as artillery pieces were concerned. We could not reply in kind, in a manner of speaking. Tanks were a special problem for us. There were every now and then two tanks that were positioned at Kranjcici and one at Cer which would drive out of the village and climb to the left, firing at every single house, and there was no way for us to neutralise that tank or jeopardise the tank's position in any way. Sometimes they would fire as many as 500 shells a day on the village and the attacks occurred on a daily basis, varying in intensity, and sometimes there were attacks coming from other directions, but those certainly were daily attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the reason for asking these questions really is to ask you: Upon what target those guns were sighted as far as you could observe from their patterns of fire. Did those guns appear to be sighted on the village of Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And prior --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- they were also sighted trained specifically on the 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 civilian population and property. The objective of those attacks was certainly to destroy as much property as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. During the time before the fighting on the 14th of September, did you ever observe the HVO firing those guns and sighting those guns on the hamlets of Uzdol in which the Croat civilians lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you -- well, I'll put the question in two ways. Did you ever notice those -- before the 14th of September, did you ever notice those guns firing on or being sighted on any of the villages of -- the hamlets within Uzdol, that being the Croat-inhabited hamlets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I've understood your question. But the answer is no, never. I was there all the time and I never noticed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But to your observation, during the morning of the 14th of September, once the action began, at least some HVO artillery began to shoot in exactly that direction, namely the direction of the Croat-inhabited hamlets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it appeared to you at least that that shelling was very heavy during the time when you were in the area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And at least some of the -- of that artillery - and I'm thinking in particular of the anti-aircraft gun - commenced firing very early on in the action that morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only in the morning, not straight away, but soon afterwards. After the fighting had started, soon after that. And I think that it was the mortars and Howitzers that were fired rather than anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, feel free to correct any mistakes that I put, because I certainly wasn't there. Could you give an estimate the best -- and I understand it will only be a rough estimate. But could you give an estimate as to how long between the starting of the fighting and the starting of the artillery fire that you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I want to ask you some questions about smoke and the presence of smoke. Is it the fact that the explosion of the shells combined with the burning of certain buildings in the hamlets produced a significant amount of smoke in the area of Uzdol? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. You can use smoke mines or -- but without that, yes, there would be smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And does that accord with your memory looking out -- when you did have the chance to look out over the area of Uzdol at any stage during the combat, did you notice yourself a significant amount of smoke to be present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was a lot of smoke and a lot of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now you've indicated that there was artillery fire and smoke. I want to ask you: As far as you could see and hear in the places that you were, did that state of affairs continue throughout the battle at Uzdol, namely that there was a lot of artillery fire and a lot of smoke in the area of the battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at around 12.00 there was a counter-attack by the HVO and that there was a withdrawal after that of the units of the army from the village. And after that, perhaps an hour or so later, there was artillery fire towards the village of Here and it went on for almost the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But I think I'm really asking you the question about conditions in the hamlets of Uzdol between about 5.30 a.m. and about 10.00 a.m. in the morning, in that time period. Would you agree with this that: During that time, there was a great deal of smoke, a great deal of burning fire on buildings, and a great many artillery shells falling during that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, you've given clear evidence that you yourself did not personally enter any of the hamlets where deceased --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- persons had been found. But were you in a position to hear from where you were the fact that there was small arms fire, in other words hand-held guns, gunfire coming from those villages and also -- sorry and including among those villages, the village of Cer where the school was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could hear the sounds of fighting all over; it resounded and you could clearly hear it. There was artillery fire that resounded and infantry weapons fire as well. And you could smell the smell of burning and gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So to the best of your observation, what you were watching or what you saw and what you took part in was a battle. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, are you going to tender this document, I mean the photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, I am. And would you just allow me to see if I eve finished the question. Yes, I offer that document for tender now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D451.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I understand the time has come to move on from that question. I'm move on from that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I've want to ask you some questions about the action. Before you went into the action, were some of the soldiers -- and including yourself, concerned at the danger that you might be fired upon out of those houses in the hamlets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew on the basis of our reconnoitring that we had done regularly from the hill, Kostajnica which you have on the image in front of you if you're looking at the same village. So you could see the whole of the village of Uzdol and you could also see that there was some soldiers in the inhabited houses, they were put up there. They weren't all in the school. But how many soldiers exactly was never established. So of course we expected a battle amongst and around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And indeed you foresaw a danger of house-to-house fighting when you went in there -- sorry, not when you went into the villages. I'll put the question again. You foresaw a danger of house-to-house fighting for those soldiers when they went into the villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to return to -- go to the topic of first of all the question of uniforms. It was not the practice of the Prozor Independent Battalion to wear a green uniform with a green beret on top, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The members of the Independent Prozor Battalion didn't wear that. What they wore were camouflage uniforms for the most part, like the rest of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just in terms of green berets, to your knowledge there was a famous unit back in Sarajevo in 1992 which was called the Green Berets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that was quite famous on the television. In fact, it had featured in news broadcasts and so on very early on in the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But yourself you yourself did not see any soldiers wearing green uniforms with green berets going into battle in Uzdol on the 14th of September, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were all dressed the same way. We all had camouflage uniforms, the patterned type of uniform, without berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to move to the question of some police. I'm going to give you a list of names. Are you familiar with an individual called Dzevad Korbadzic -- Corbadzic, sorry, pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzevad Corbadzic, yes, the name seems familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Aziz Bobar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sabahudin Motika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And another person, Kasim Hujdur.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a man like that, but I don't know if that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm specifically not referring to Enes Hujdur but a Hujdur who was a member of the police, the civilian police. Do you know such a man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And to your understanding what is his first name? I've put it as Kasim here. But is that your understanding of his first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about Kasim because there is a Kasim Hujdur but I don't know if he was deployed in the police then at the time, so I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. To clarify -- my questions sometimes cause the trouble. As far as you remember there was a person called Hujdur in the civilian police at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And also was there a person called Sabitovic - I don't have a first name for that person - in the police force, the civilian police force at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether he was in the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you know the person to which I'm referring, Mr. Sabitovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's familiar, but as I say I can't remember his first name at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, of those people, you've indicated that you're not sure if Mr. Sabitovic was deployed in the police, but the other four, Corbadzic, Bobar, Motika, and Hujdur, were in the civilian police at the time of the fighting in Uzdol on the 14th of September. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I think they were members of the Ministry of the Interior. They were members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And those individuals fought in the battle or took part in the action at Uzdol on the morning of the 14th of September. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that the army and the police took part together in this operation, so I assume they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now, of the names that I've given you the senior figure among them was Aziz Bobar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the ones you enumerated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Who was the senior -- yes, perhaps I should have been clearer about that. To your understanding, who was the senior person from the MUP police who took part in this battle? Was it Aziz Bobar or somebody higher up than him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the police, as in the army, there was the chief of MUP, for example, who planned their deployment but did not take part like our commander who plans and orders but does not himself take part. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Are you able to recall now who was the chief of MUP who planned the police's deployment on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to tell, this is a simple question and answer. The use of the police or the deployment of the police was planned by our commander, Enver Buza, because he gave permission to the policemen how they were to move around, when they were to go, when they were to return, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But who was the person -- who was the senior police MUP operative in the area at that time, if you know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for a long time the chief of the police was Midhat Cadic [phoen]; however, I'm not sure whether he was there then, whether he was the chief then. I'm not sure and I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you see any written documentation that passed between the Prozor Independent Battalion and the MUP at the time permitting civilian police to be used in the action?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there is interference on the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The Defence notes as well that I'm receiving a horrendous mixture of my voice and other voices through the headphones at the moment. Would it help if I asked the question again? Your Honour, I'm still getting my own golden tones --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note there is interference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can answer and tell you that I never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: B/C/S on English channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We have some mix-ups in the headphones now. Your Honours, I'm now on another channel all together it seems. Maybe things have righted themselves. I'll try to continue. We'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. My apologies, Witness G. These things do happen. Okay. So as to the basis upon which the civilian police took part in this action, as far as you could see those -- sorry, not as far as you could see. Let me ask you a preliminary question. Were you personally with any civilian police yourself during your part in this battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did Commander Buza break his rule or break his usual practice and discuss with you in any detail on what basis he was allowed to use the civilian police or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I could say is this: It was common knowledge that the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence frequently and in other places used forces for operations. Now, I don't know exactly. All I can say is that our commander very often complained to our functionaries in the Ministry of the Interior and said that they weren't in fact fighting. He would criticise them and say they were being used away from the front lines. So he would criticise them for being in a safe area and they weren't exposed to danger sufficiently if they had been involved, and that this emanating from the nature of their job, that is being policemen, that they were to introduce law and order and to provide law and order on the territory of the municipality. So I'm not sure whether there was any official agreement between the two ministries or not or if it was decided at some local level. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, if you can't say I won't -- have I -- have I really exhausted your knowledge about that topic with these questions now? If so, I won't ask you any more about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what questions you have in mind, what's coming. I'm ready to answer any question of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you were fairly busy because you had a number of dead, wounded, and possibly missing as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, we did have several missing persons, and the situation during those first days wasn't settled. We knew about four or five people or soldiers who had gone missing. There was several wounded persons. And immediately after the operation, I travelled to Zenica to visit some wounded there. And I remember one soldier in particular who was from the Sutjeska Battalion. I don't know his name. He was a fair, blond person. He was wounded somewhere around his shoulder, and there was some other people there like that, too. They were in Zenica in the hospital there, and I went to visit hem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So were you movements in the battle effectively this: In the afternoon of the battle when the shelling was going on in the village of Here, you went about your business of finding out who was dead, wounded, and missing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And was it the following day that you went to Zenica or did you perform those functions on the following day as well, namely chasing up the dead, wounded, and missing, and speaking to them and their families?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day I went back to the battalion headquarters in Dobro Polje, the command there. And we were dealing with the situation there because we expected to pull out. We expected some soldiers to pull out the following day. And we could establish our casualties with any exactitude only one or two days later. So that in situations of that kind the most important thing is to contact the family of the persons killed and to organise assistance to the wounded. That's what we did or that's what my service did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Just to get an idea of when it was that you went to Zenica, was that on the third day that you went up to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether it was the third day. We had to go from Prozor to Jablanica, difficult terrain, to get some logistics. I was waiting for a helicopter to take me there and I went there by helicopter. So I can't say if it was three or four days when the first flight started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. And just to clarify the Zenica situation, is there a hospital at Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that. All right. In those three or four days immediately following the battle I take it you had no dealings with the local civilian police who had been involved in the battle. Is that correct? Or were some of them wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that some of them were wounded, but I didn't contact them much either. I was too taken up with my own affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it you didn't have any authority or competence to deal with the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, quite. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, I just want to turn now to some of the things that you heard after the battle from the soldiers in the Independent Prozor Battalion. Once the soldiers of the Bosnian army had retreated, is it the fact that not one of those soldiers told you that there had been murders of any innocent civilians? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Some of the soldiers, though, did report having to fight with armed civilians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases like that. There was a case over there like that, and I think it involved an elderly person who had a gun and shot, something like that. Just one case. I know about this one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Are you able now -- and I understand it's 11 years later, but just do the best you can. Can you recall which village -- which hamlet that particular case of the old man shooting with the gun occurred in? Understanding that you were just going on what you were told, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the hamlet of Kriz, which is where the two wounded army members were who were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just tell us a little bit about that. You I've indicated two wounded army members were pulled out from Kriz. Was -- first of all, how bad -- what was the wounds that those individuals suffered to the best of your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was wounded in the area of the shoulder; I've already said that. And the other had an entrance/exit wound through both his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the shooting was lateral if it managed to hit both legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And just -- because we weren't there, we don't have the same information. It appeared to you that they were bullet wounds. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct. Without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. I understand. All right. Now, apart from those -- now, apart from those two wounded who were pulled out of the village of Kriz, how many other wounded were taken up to the hospital at Zenica, to the best of your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another person. Only those who were seriously wounded were taken to Zenica and the others remained. One person had sustained face injuries. There was an entry-and-exit wound through the lower part of his jaw. Those people would be taken to the hospital, and those who were less seriously wounded would stay behind at the war hospital in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The man who had the injury to his jaw, do you know which part of Uzdol he was in when he received that injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He wasn't able to speak. Even today he has trouble speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And as to those who were wounded in a less serious way, are you now able to recall whereabouts in Uzdol they were when they got injured? I appreciate this may be a difficult one to remember, but there may be a detail that you recall and if you do would you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that those who were slightly wounded, those who had suffered grazes or scratches, were less important at the time. We didn't pay much attention to that. They weren't sufficiently important to use the few medical supplies that we had for them. Those were people who were just slightly wounded, and this was not actually something that we kept track of. As for serious wounds, entry-and-entrance wounds, and deep cuts, the people who suffered those types of wounds had to be sent to a hospital and away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you very much for that. Now, I just want to ask you a question very quickly about the reliability of the news broadcasts that you received. You've already answered questions about this, so I just want to limit it to this: Back in those days, September of 1993 and the adjoining months, was it the practice of the extreme elements of the HVO to release claims on a very frequent basis of disgusting war crimes by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say -- I must be absolutely open and truthful. This was never broadcast on the local radio station, Rama, the radio station in Prozor. Once we come to other areas, I'm sure there was a veritable flood of both information and misinformation to the effect that the Bosniaks were attacking the Croat civilian population, committing crimes, especially in the area of Konjic; and we knew this to be a lie. The Croatian television went as far as to actually fabricate reports by a journalist called Smiljko Sagolj about a Bosnian village like Glognica having been burned. He had his picture taken right there, claiming that he was in fact in Kostanjica, whereas he was in a different village. Misinformation was spread in this way, and as a result the public was misinformed. This had a lot of negative effects and let further clashes. There was a veritable flood of misinformation concerning such crimes; that much is certain. However, this was not possible in the case of Prozor. To this very day we don't know about any crimes that were committed against the Croatian population in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And which media outlet was it on which you first heard any news of these claims that civilians, innocent civilians, had been massacred by the Bosnian army during the battle at Prozor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this action or in a more general sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I mean this particular action.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local radio station called Rama -- this was actually announced two or three days later. All I can say about these reports is that this radio station was also used for spreading propaganda, in my opinion. The same radio station spread a lot of other reports from areas further off. It was very difficult to believe everything they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And indeed you were a person who could have had no such information because you didn't go to those villages, Kriz, Rajici, Zelenike, and the other smaller ones nearby. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And of course the soldiers who you were with must have known very well exactly what your part was, namely to fight in the front line for a little while and then become involved in helping wounded soldiers get back to safety. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They knew that my involvement had to do with morale and not so much with combat. Everyone was aware of it, or most of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In fact, all you had was a pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So then finally on that topic, it's the fact -- there was no use for anyone to ask you about the killings of those civilians, and no one did ask you about them in that period of time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was, but the truth is no one asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now I just ask that the witness be shown a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's going to be shown to you now is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's D149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This document I'm about to show you is a combat report, a report from -- by Enver Buza who was the commander of the Independent Prozor Battalion to the command of the 6th Corps. And I would just like you to -- just look at the screen and you'll see this all to come up. Okay. I would just ask you to read that document, please. I've got some questions for you about it, but just read over it, noting who it's sent by, who it's sent to, and noting also its contents, and then I'm going to ask you some questions about it. Now, just as you read through it one of the questions I will ask you is: Have you ever seen this document before? I'm not presuming that you have, but just as you look and assimilate the material in it, you may be able to comment whether you have or you haven't. When you need the screen to be adjusted, please say so and the court staff will help you with that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before, but it's nothing unexpected. The commander wrote whatever he pleased and requested whatever he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well -- yes, of course. And there was no need for Commander Buza to show you this document even if he had have been in a good relationship with you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I've got the English version in front of me. Do you have -- Sorry, just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you have the whole document in front of you on one sheet of paper? The reason I ask is I'm working from an English translation, which goes into two pages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the whole document on the screen, but I can see sections of it at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you had the chance to read the first part? And if you have, we'll move the screen down to the next part.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm about to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Witness G, I'm not looking at what you're looking at. I've got an English version and you've got a Bosnian version there. Do you need the screen to be scrolled down so that you can see more, or have you now read the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right. I've read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Well, you've never seen that document before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, nevertheless on the face of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, just be careful. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for the warning, Your Honour. Yes, sorry about that. Could that just be redacted, please. Thank you for the warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now -- now I've got some questions about that. First of all, as a matter of substance, do you notice that towards the end of the document there is a reference to -- as follows: "The armed soldiers and civilians in the surrounding villages even held armed women in front of themselves and started to put up resistance. Fire was returned. The entire Uzdol, Here, Kute, and Scipe sector was under heavy artillery fire." Now, I understand you didn't tell Commander Buza that. What I'm asking you is: As far as you know, who did Commander Buza speak to before he wrote this report? I'm not asking you to comment on the accuracy of it; I'll come to that in a minute. But first of all, who were the people to your knowledge that Buza did speak to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing I know is he didn't speak to me. I left the area soon afterwards. He must have spoken to the commanders of those combat groups, and he makes reference here to the units that were involved. He must have spoken to their commanders and received reports from them. What I can say, based on what people were saying at the time, basically it was being said at the time that this report might as well be quite accurate. There is reference here to 65 soldiers and 13 civilians. What I can say is that people were saying there were more casualties on the Croatian side; I'm not sure if that's accurate or not because people were also saying that in Uzdol there had been members of the regular Croatian military forces. I'm not sure if that's true or not. If they'd had -- if they'd suffered any casualties, those certainly were not entered in regular HVO reports for the simple reason that those people were members of an altogether different army. As for civilians, armed or not, it's a relative question. It's very difficult to discuss it on these terms, if you have in mind the conditions that prevailed at the time. It was difficult under such heavy artillery fire to ascertain who the civilians were and who the soldiers were. It was difficult to even establish if people were carrying any firearms or not. There was a lot of smoke and a whole lot of shooting going on. It was very hard to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, thank you for that. Now, I've got -- I've asked you some questions about the substance of that document; now I've got a couple of questions about the form of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can the document please be scrolled up to the top so Witness G can see the addressing and so on. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, you observed that that document appears to be addressed by Enver Buza.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And does it appear to you to be addressed to the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that in the up right corner. No doubt about that, it was addressed to the command of the 6th Corps. The document clearly reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And although at the bottom of the document there's -- well, perhaps I'll come to what's at the bottom of the document in a second. Let's stay with that. It's addressed to the 6th Corps, and to your knowledge the 6th Corps was the corps in which the Independent Prozor Battalion was subordinated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want you to look at the first line of the text where it says: "Pursuant to attack order operative order 01/1500-27 of 11 September 1993." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, as you understand the position, when a commander writes an order like this he indicates, as Commander Buza has done here, what was the source of his power, of his authority, to commit offensive operations. And -- well, perhaps that was a speech-like question and I'll just withdraw that question. I'm sorry. I'll ask a better one. Do you see the numbers there, the operative number of the order. It's 01/1500-27. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. That is the first line, and that indeed is the order that he appears to be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. And that order number should allow the identification of the actual order which Commander Buza was obeying when he sent the Prozor Battalion into battle on the 14th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I think my learned friend's counsel has taken this witness as far as he can in respect of some of the questions with respect to this document. I don't think the witness is in a position to answer about this particular reference number, where it comes from. He simply hasn't seen the document before. I can see where learned counsel is going, but in this respect, as I said, I think he has taken it as far as he can and I will object to that last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's a very difficult for this witness to answer, unless you lay down some foundations for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I will lay down a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But certainly in your proofing session with the learned Prosecutor you weren't shown this document, were you, or given a chance to comment on it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. But nevertheless, you're familiar with the system of giving numbers to orders so that those orders can be subsequently identified. Is that correct? That's a system you've seen -- well, perhaps I'll ask that question first and then I'll ask another.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you've seen other combat reports in on other occasions unrelated to this of a similar nature which identify the authorising order by number. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I have seen plenty of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And so, according to the system of -- to the military system and the system of numbering on orders, if we go and look at operative number 01/1500-27, we'll find the order that Buza was obeying when he sent the troops into battle. Is that how you understand the system to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this report appears to indicate. You have the protocol number, the date, the date in relation to this document dated the 11th of September, and that's when this order should be dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown another document now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before that, could we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could I just indicate for the assistance of everyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- we are perhaps two documents and a ten-minute burst away from the finish of this cross-examination. So we have very nearly finished, but it's probably got another 15, 20 minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we'll have a break now and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now could the witness please be shown the Exhibit D152.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's going to come up on the screen now is an order which has got the same number on it as the one referred to in -- in the Buza report. Now, the questions I have for you about this document may be quite limited, and in fact they may be limited to one question only, frankly. And the first question is going to be: Have you ever seen this document before? Would you just take a moment to read it over and indicate whether you've ever seen it before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Well, I think under those circumstances that will be the end of the questions on that document. Very well. Thanks. Just excuse me. There's one other document I would just like you to have a look at, please. Yes, perhaps -- sorry, there was one thing I wanted to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could please -- I apologise to the court staff for this. Could we go back to the previous document, and that was D149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm just going to go back to the Buza combat report for a moment, Witness G, and just going to ask you to comment on one part of it. While it's up on the screen, I want to ask you: When Sefer Halilovic came along and was angry with Buza for not departing, did Sefer leave behind when he left a person from the inspection teams -- oh, you don't know about inspection teams, sorry -- called Zicro Suljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And was that person, Zicro Suljevic, a person who you met the following day in a cellar in a bombed house in Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just -- before I come back to that document, too, I'll just ask you a question about -- about Buza and Suljevic. Was it your understanding that during the fighting operation undertaken by the Bosnian army that morning that Buza and Suljevic took up position in an observation post up on the hill of Krstiste? I'm sorry, my pronunciation of that is terrible, I know, but Krstiste.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they were, but I assume that they might have been around Krstiste hill. But I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've just got a question for you, too, about the communications equipment available to the attacking soldiers from the Bosnian army. Firstly, did you visit this or any command post or observation post on the hill of Krstiste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hill of Krstiste was no command post. It was the outmost position controlled by the BH army. I had been there countless times, that's for sure. During the operation, however, I assume it may have been selected to serve that purpose because it gives a good view of the area. I can't be certain, however, if the commander was there or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you saw Mr. Suljevic in that cellar, was that cellar serving as some sort of command headquarters or was that cellar serving as a place to hide from the bombs and the shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Zicro Suljevic was there. I didn't see the commander there. I mean Buza. It was just a regular cellar where you could take cover from the shells. It was just a regular cellar in a house where there was nothing much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that puts an end to one part of my questions about the communication equipment. How many radios did -- if any, did the Bosnian troops have when they set off earlier in the morning to go and perform their duties and attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen a single piece myself, but I do believe they had several, two or three at most. Secondly, the problem with those hand-held radios was that they were entirely unprotected in terms of communication. They were all too easy to locate and listen into. It's the least secure means of communication. And those were short-range devices and they couldn't be operated for very long because the batteries used were very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to those two or three radios, do you know which persons had those radios? Was it combat leaders or platoon leaders, company leaders? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I assume it must have been the combat group commanders. I'm not sure that these radios were distributed establishment-wise. It was only for that occasion that they were assigned to combat group commanders. I guess it might have been only them who might have been in possession of those two or three radios that we had to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But what you can say with your certain knowledge is that normal soldiers of the line or the basic fighting soldiers did not have radios?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means, no. No way. It would have been impossible. I'm not even sure about all of the commanders, but it's possible. There weren't that many radios to go around for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, on the screen -- on that screen on the very end of that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In the English version could we have page 2 and could the witness please be given the chance to look at the bottom end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We're just going to look at the end of the document. Okay. Now, it's apparent, isn't it, that this document here concludes with a piece of information that this report and the overall data have been made available to SVK chief, Sefer Halilovic, Colonel Vehbija Karic, and Colonel Zicro Suljevic who monitored the whole operation from the observation post." Do you see that passage there? It's the last thing said before the signature of Buza.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear about what that all actually means. The fact of the matter is to your knowledge, it was Zicro Suljevic, not Halilovic or Karic, who were actually present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. In our part, yes. Where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And it's apparent there although this is a combat report to the 6th Corps and made pursuant to a particular order with a particular order number, that the information was also made available to Halilovic, Karic, and Suljevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it would appear from this document. Now, whether they actually received it or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, yes, look I'm going along with elephant-like steps, but my last question on that topic is: You had nothing to do with communicating the contents of this document to Halilovic, Suljevic, or Karic yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you indicated on Friday that your knowledge about the role of Halilovic stemmed from a couple of factors which you described at the time, one of which was the explanation given by Commander Buza after the Dobro Polje meeting on the 5th of September. And do you recall that evidence that you gave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But to your knowledge the Independent Prozor Battalion was never resubordinated out of the organic structure of the 6th Corps of the Bosnian army. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, when it comes to the 6th Corps or units of the BH army in the territory of our municipality, I can say this: At the beginning of 1992 there was a sort of mixed pattern. But when the 6th Corps was established until the corps itself was disbanded, it was -- I don't know that we were resubordinated to anyone, but during a period of time during 1992 we did have two superior commands of some sort at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm really talking about 1993. In the time -- sorry -- well, perhaps I should ask you this: In the days before the 6th Corps was formed, were you part of the 4th Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after that, when the 6th Corps was formed you were part of the 6th Corps -- by "you" I mean the Independent Prozor Battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that's where the Independent Prozor Battalion stayed until the 6th Corps was dissolved at some time in 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisationally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm asking you about, formally speaking. Yes, very well. Now, I think I've nearly finished the questions. Just excuse me one moment, I just want to check a couple of things and then I think I have finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could that please be redacted. Your Honours, I apologise for that. It's a refined version of the problem that I encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Anyway, in the position that you held at the time, Witness G, was it part of your responsibility to send combat reports or any other kind of reports from the Independent Prozor Battalion to the 6th Corps, or was that the job of some other official within the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my job to send combat reports, and I could not prepare combat reports. All I could perhaps do is to prepare some other kind of report if there was another problem that arose. But never combat reports, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. In that event I won't show you the combat reports log. Okay. After the action was finished and during the time in the days after the 14th of September, did you personally go to the village of Voljevac at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there a number of times privately because my family or part of my family was accommodated there for a time. So I would go there frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. In those trips did you become aware of the anger towards Commander Buza that was -- that was held by fighters in the 45th Brigade who had lost comrades in the battle of Crni Vrh on the 13th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that anger, yes, and the disillusionment. I encountered that more on another territory rather than Voljevac because the brigade very frequently moved to its own area. So I would go there frequently. It's the area of -- what's it called? The municipality of Buturovic Polje. So it was at the command there of the 45th that I met the commander and other people from the brigade. And I do know about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether or not Sefer Halilovic and also Vehbija Karic proposed in the wake of the Uzdol attack that from that time on Enver Zejnilagic should have a commanding role, not just over his own 317th Brigade, but also over neighbouring brigades including the Independent Prozor Battalion? Did you become aware of any such proposal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was even shown a document I think here by the Prosecution that speaks about that. I think it was -- I thinks the date was the 15th of September, so I know about that. But yes, there were thoughts along those lines earlier on, too, that from the Independent Prozor Battalion and another battalion from Gornji Vakuf that a separate brigade should be formed. However, that was just the idea. It was never put into practice. There was always this idea of making it a separate operational direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, could I just ask that the witness please be shown -- excuse me one moment. Sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness please be shown a document -- before -- sorry. Sorry, just excuse me. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Could the witness please be shown P124.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The document that you're going to be shown now is a document under the hand of Sefer Halilovic, it's an order, and it's dated 15th September 1993. And I just want you to clarify whether this is the document you were shown by the Prosecutor or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. And you notice that that document bears the date 15th September. How many times does it say "15th September" on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But could the witness please now be shown D158, and could this document please be shown to all of the court in its original in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just looking at that document there, were you shown this document by the Prosecution when you were being proofed here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether this is the same document that I was shown a moment ago. If it isn't -- if it's not the same, then I wasn't shown it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I appreciate there are some similarities in the text, which we know about. But just looking at it now, would you look at the signature part. Do you see that it says "Sefer Halilovic" in the typewritten copy on the bottom right? Yeah. Do you see it says "for" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Does it appear to you to say "for Sefer Halilovic" and the handwritten signature appears to be Karic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, but of course I can't confirm whether Karic signed this. But I do see the fact that Halilovic didn't sign this document; somebody signed it for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would you look up to the top left, please, where the dates are to be seen. And do you notice up there that the date of the 15th of the ninth occurs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And how many times does it appear to occur on this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see it once here, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you see there are -- in the top left there's a -- it says "Voljevac 15/9/93." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes, and that's all I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you see the handwritten section just immediately below it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, I can see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There you have, once again in handwriting, "15/9/93." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I was looking for the date further down the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay. All right. Thank you very much for that. Now, after the battle was over and while you were doing your duties, it was the expectation of you and I suggest also some of your fellow fighters that the HVO was very likely to counter-attack in that area as soon as they could. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could assume that, yes, and that is correct. That's what we expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But although there was shelling of the village and sporadic action, in that particular area there was no further full-scale fighting in the week following the battle on the 14th of September, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not there but during my previous testimony I said that the HVO had tried several times to take control of the village of Here, and one of those attempts was on the 22nd of January, 1993. And afterwards, after that, I can't tell you exactly how many times the infantry started -- tried to attack and take control, but there was some sort of ludicrous reports by our commander, company commander, to the effect that a strong artillery attack supported by the infantry was carried out, which is a little strange, that the infantry should support the artillery. But anyway, there was several attempts after the 15th of September until the end of the year. There weren't any such attempts anymore. They were mostly attacks from a distance, artillery attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that was my last question, but I've just another one. You mentioned the 22nd of January, 1993. I take it you meant really the 22nd of January, 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the 22nd --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you mean 1993? In other words, did you -- I just -- I'm sorry. It may be that my questions have caused trouble here. The attack that you've referred to that took place on the 22nd of January, is that before or after the Uzdol battle that we've been talking about here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before the battle, so it was the 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, the village of Here fell on the 24th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's another attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: My apologies for that self-righteous correction. And I have now finished my cross-examination. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
