utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just a few clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. You were down D149.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could that please be brought on to the screen, court deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you remember that document? Well, you remember being shown this particular document when --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would like, please, if the Bosnian version could be shown on for the Judges to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You will be shown the document in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to indicate that I was stopped in cross-examining on this document because of the witness's ability to know about it and to see it. And there's no question asked yet, but if there's going to be expert commentary sought, then I would object to it because the Prosecutor stopped me effectively on that very basis. So if that's what's coming, it's going to be objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We haven't heard the question yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And for the record, I stopped that or I objected to it at a stage after a lot of questions had been asked. But nevertheless, I think this needs some clarification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you look at that document and then at the very front, you see there are a lot of things being crossed out. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, from your own knowledge, what would that -- all those things which have been crossed out mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says "A/A" means that the document was placed in the archives of the Prozor Independent Battalion. This other portion, I don't know what that is, these slanty lines. And I don't know what these numbers are here either. On one part in the upper left-hand corner it says the sector for military security, which means it was sent separate to that sector, the sector for military security. I assume it was the sector in the command of the 6th Corps, the sector for military security.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where it says "commander," which is on the right-hand side, that has also be crossed out, commander of the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, is my friend giving evidence about this, making a statement that that's been crossed out? There's no evidence at all about those lines or their meaning or their provenance. But if my friend wants to ask the witness about how those lines got to be there, I have no objection. If he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes -- I think it's also helpful for you to know the reason on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I agree entirely, but I don't want the witness to be put in a position of answering about questions he doesn't know about it. So it's got to be established he does know about it and if he does, he can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness is an extremely intelligent one and he can tell us whether he knows or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, the objection is not to the witness or his intelligence, it's to the question of my learned friend. My friend could perhaps ask the appropriate question and then perhaps I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Where it says, Witness G, "commander of the 6th Corps," there's some lines through that. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that means. It says "the command of the 6th Corps." Somebody might have -- somebody could have crossed it out before it was sent or after it was sent. So I really can't say. I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Neither can you assist the Chamber, can you, with whether the command of the 6th Corps actually got this particular document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they received it or not, and I can't say on the basis of this whether the document was stored or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Thank you. That's all from this particular document. Now, the other question you were asked by learned counsel for the Defence was -- was whether the Prozor Independent Battalion was subordinated during this operation, during this offensive in Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think that wasn't the question at all. There was a question asked effectively -- and in fact it was a trio of questions. When did you go into the 6th Corps, when did you leave the 6th Corps; and did you stay in the 6th Corps in the meantime. Those were the questions. I remember them pretty well. I haven't got it on the screen in front of me now. If those matters need to be clarified, the answers did look rather clear, but that might be just my view rather than my friend's. If she wishes to clarify any specific of those, there's no objection. But to phrase it the way she did doesn't truly state what I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there must be some summarisation of the questions you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I agree. I don't want to cause a war over this topic. I agree there has to be some summarisation, and maybe my friend knows better than me what I meant, but I don't think so. Anyway, Your Honour, if you're minded to accept the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Perhaps it will help counsel if I quote directly what he did ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: "The Prozor Independent Battalion was never resubordinated out of the organic structure of the 6th Corps." Do you remember being asked that particular question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said that since its establishment, the 6th Corps was always within the composition of that corps, that it wasn't resubordinated to anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time that whether any other -- whether any units were subordinated for the purposes of this offensive in Neretva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I knew was that along our direction and axis, that there would be a slight change and that the 45th Brigade would come to our assistance. Now, which units would be resubordinated or subordinated, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you did not have all the information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you given information about subordination of units during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't -- or let me explain. I worked -- I did a quite different job. This is the operative part of the business, if a unit is subordinated and taken from one area of responsibility to another. That wasn't within the realm of my work. It wasn't the duty of the commander to inform me about that. He was my immediate superior officer from whom I received the most important information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Witness G. Now, I'll go -- I'll ask some other clarifications and I'll start from the very beginning, and I'll try to follow the chronology as was done by counsel for the Defence. You were asked whether you yourself had feelings of revenge against the local Croats. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And I believe you answered: "No, never." But the question now is: To your knowledge, could the same be said of other soldiers who, as we have heard, suffered at the hands of the HVO which were in the Prozor Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say what other people felt. Sometimes it's difficult to say what even my closest friends feel. It's a difficult call. I know that until September 1993 the Bosniak population had been subjected to measures of military force that were unheard of in our area. If you ask me about the feelings of the families of those who were the victims of this situation, all I can say is I can't talk about that. Perhaps you should ask them. But one thing I can say is that there was a heated situation in that area, and it was precisely on account of the crimes that had occurred up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness G. Now, the other question you were asked was about what the official position was about atrocities against civilians by the army. And you said that it was quite clear within the BiH army no atrocities against civilians were to be committed. Do you remember now? And I am paraphrasing here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, did you hear this being said to the soldiers at any time, that this is our official position and we do not wish to have any atrocities against the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness I think gave evidence that he said it himself to the soldiers. Now, you've got to be a bit careful about re-examination to clarify. I don't object to clarification. This appears to me to be a second go, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not my memory that the witness himself said it. Perhaps we can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask the witness on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Will you please answer that, Witness G, whether such a thing was relayed to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only were the soldiers told, not only was this relayed to them, what's more we had specific examples. I remember the attempted rape of a Croatian lady in our municipality. The soldier responsible was punished severely. Word got around throughout the Independent Battalion. Later, we introduced special measures to protect the civilian population throughout the territory controlled by the Prozor Independent Battalion. I spoke about this police checkpoint that was manned around the clock protecting the population of the village of Ivanica from any further incidents of this nature happening. That was after this incident occurred. Not only did people talk about this. I spoke to my soldiers about it personally on a number of occasions, and we set an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before the soldiers -- I'm talking at a more specific time, which is the 13th of September, when the Prozor Independent Battalion had been given some talks in -- when we were addressed by both Sefer Halilovic and Enver Buza. Was this ever mentioned, about the civilian population and how they are to be treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much was said about the civilian population, and few thoughts were spared them generally speaking. In order for my testimony to be entirely truthful and accurate, I must admit that the most important thing for all of us was to carry out the tasks that we had been assigned, and I mean military tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness G. Now, the other question was -- and I'm sure I'm not going to pronounce this correctly. This is about these two Bosnian words and you said: I was not informed about the role of the inspection team or General Halilovic. And "lead the action" is the word used. And you said "rukovodjenje" was not used and you distinguished the word "rukovoditi" and "voditi." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I believe I spoke about a different thing. When an order is written down, then the phrasing is very important. If you just write the general term "order," that's one thing. If you write: "I hereby order," that is far more serious and far more binding.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was this in the context of the order that you saw on Enver Buza's desk?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be -- I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: For a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can bring that document up and see what exactly the word was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the witness certified that he only had a glance over that order. I believe that you have to ask to this witness whether the witness remembered which word on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I will ask -- I'm grateful for your guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness G, did you notice which word had been used, if you recall of course, when you saw that document on Enver Buza's desk that you have seen? Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that I don't remember the entire document; that's what I said. It's very difficult to use that particular document to test my recollection now. I spoke about the document that was shown me here, and what it states in no uncertain terms is the term order. And it doesn't say "I hereby order." It's a document that I think was signed by General Halilovic. It says "order," generically, and not "I hereby order." Whereas I can't really recall what the document that I saw at the time, that I glanced over in Enver Buza's office indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, is it normal to give orders -- I'll take that back. Can I begin again. What, in your view, is the difference between an order, direction, and guidance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a military background myself. The only way to answer your question is to use my own educational background and training, such background as I had studying those matters in passing, in a manner of speaking. An order is very specific. Direction and guidance would be a different thing altogether, but I'm not sure I can really answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Witness G, in reply to Defence counsel's question you stated that you were not clear whether it was an order or a proposal. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're speaking about now. Which document are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This same document that you saw on Enver Buza's desk.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for the document that I saw on Enver Buza's table, I only spoke about the section that indicated where the Prozor Independent Battalion was supposed to go. There's nothing else that I can say about it. I'm telling you what's lodged in my memory based on a fleeting glance, and that was the only section that I ever focused on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And in your experience as to where a battalion was supposed to go, would that be contained in a proposal or an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, there's three objections to that. The first one is that it need not be that you have to choose. It might be that what's being put in a leading form is that -- and I'll use the terms my learned friend did. "Would that be contained in a proposal or an order" is a dichotomy that need not be acceptable. It might be that it be contained in one, both, or neither. And my learned friend is not entitled in re-examination to put a cross-examining question. However, there is another objection. The objection is now that my friend is now seeking to get expert evidence from this witness, having effectively preventing me from doing that, I would submit that it's objectionable to do that and I object on both of those bases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult for me to say anything on this occasion. Maybe you could put your question another way taking into consideration the objections from Mr. Morrissey, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I would like to state that I don't think I'm asking the witness for an expert opinion. And I'm asking the similar kind of questions that Mr. Morrissey put to this witness in regard to his general experience as a military man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we noticed that that is -- you just ask this witness himself as a military man's opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Witness G, can you tell us when military troops are to move for combat and there's a document, what kind of a document would it be before military units would move into battle? What would be the normal format used for such movement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a unit to be committed, for a unit to commence activity, there would need to be an order for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness G. Now, moving on to another area. You were asked my learned counsel for the Defence about the information Enver Buza would give you, and you have said it was not very much. Now, you stated to a question that normally information from Enver Buza was superficial, not thorough, and incomplete. Is that the correct position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness G, was it your experience that Enver Buza, although reticent, would give you wrong information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Enver Buza is a liar. He did that countless times. He lied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And would he lie about information about where troops had to go to battle and when the combat was supposed to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how that question could be asked or answered, and I object to it. It just is not a question that can elicit a meaningful answer, frankly, and I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I see no problem about this question because the witness's answered triggered this question. In this situation, this kind of question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness G, would he lie to you about combat and whether the troops would be going into combat? Would he lie about those kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a document that I was shown here. It's a combat report by our commander, and I spotted a lie in an official document like that. That's where it says that our right flank neighbour remained inactive and there were no sounds of fighting going on to our right; that just wasn't true and yet the combat report stated precisely that. It's very difficult for me to speak about what he could have said and what he would not have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Witness G, that -- another question you were asked by learned counsel for the Defence was whether you drew the conclusion that Sefer Halilovic was the commander of the operation because of what Buza told you. And you answered: "On the whole, yes." Can you explain what you meant by: "On the whole, yes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, over ten years have gone by. It's been 12 years since those events took place. Over these 11 years, a lot of thoughts have crossed my mind. It's very difficult for me to say now -- it's very difficult for me to go back to that day and place and recall the exact words used by our commander. But roughly speaking, that was our only source of information, what our commander told us on that occasion. Please try to understand that so much time has gone by and it's very hard for me, if not impossible, to quote his exact words. I prefer to say that having in mind General Halilovic's previous position, it was more a case of inertia, as something being tacitly Realtime transcript read in error: "taskedly"] understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said inertia, as something tacitly understood -- it says taskedly in the script. And who was this tacitly understood by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, irrespective of what Enver Buza told you, from your own observation what was your perception as to who was in charge of this offensive in Neretva?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. The witness has indicated that there was no irrespective of what Enver Buza told him. He says he had that perception because of what Mr. Buza told him. And it's unfair and in my submission misleading -- not improperly so, but it's a question that has that effect -- to put that to the witness as a hypothetical. To say, forget about the real basis for your understanding, what was your basis for understanding. He said what it was, and in my submission this has gone far enough. And I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may make sure whether the witness really said that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: From the record it says "and General Halilovic's previous position." So it's not only what Enver Buza said to him, just to correct what learned counsel said to you. But nevertheless I will ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what it is that you did say when you were asked this question by the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this. In my submission we're now in a fishing expedition. If my friend has something from my questioning to clarify, then it can be put to the witness. To go asking the witness what he said and to try to ask questions on that is not permissible, to keep it very short, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will still ask Witness G this question, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: From your own observation, who did you think was in charge of the offensive in Neretva?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, that question has been asked and answered now probably three times. And in my submission, he's said what his perception was, that Halilovic was the commander based on certain bases. And I'm not sure that this is anything other than an attempt to get a slightly better or different version of exactly the same thing, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think if there is no dispute with this answer, we could pass this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will then ask this next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was the most senior man in the region during this offensive in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has become evidence in-chief again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- and I object to it as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, this is evidence in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does arise directly out of. I don't mean to be argumentative in any way, and I will not ask it; but it is something that arose out of cross-examination. And I believe the witness has already stated that in examination-in-chief, so I will leave that question alone. If Your Honours will give me just a moment to collect my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Witness G, you said because of reconnoitring in the area you were area that it was an inhabited area and soldiers were living in houses. Do you remember that in response to a question from learned counsel for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you said that we expected a battle in the village, and that was before this offensive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean. You said that a battle was expected before this offensive. Was that what your question was about?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, no. You said that a battle was expected during the offensive. I'm sorry if my question was not as clear as it ought to have been.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: During, yes, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, of course -- I mean right. And you knew that soldiers would be possibly fighting in inhabited houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could merely assume no more than that. Our chief objective was to destroy any military facilities and to crush the HVO at the front end. And at the rear end of the village where they had a communications centre, there was some sort of a headquarters and all their logistics. There were hamlets in between. Those were the two preconditions to successfully complete our task.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But the point is: Was this -- was any guidance given to the Prozor Independent Battalion who was about to go into battle and into houses where they may have soldiers? Was any guidance given to them how to treat and how to react in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was entirely unpredictable that the HVO would resort to using artillery against one of their own villages. It must have come as a great surprise. Secondly, combat operations being as intense as they were, it was impossible to impart clear instructions. The clearest instruction would probably have been: Go out and fend for yourself. Perhaps I have forgotten to say one thing. I heard about this one case. It was due to the lie of the land in the area of the village. Anyway, I heard about a group of civilians running ahead to meet a group of BH army soldiers. I know that no one touched them and they were eventually released. I believe one person in that group was called Cvita Stojanovic a lady. I'm not sure if anyone else was with her. They had come across members of a military police team, and they were released. However, under the conditions of intense fighting that prevailed at the time, I say it would have been impossible to ascertain with any degree of accuracy who was a civilian and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right, Witness G. Now, the other thing the counsel for the Defence asked, you said there would be no need to ask you about the killings of the civilians after it happened and you said nobody asked you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, in the position that you had, you would talk to most of the soldiers, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fact I don't mind the witness answering this particular question from his own knowledge, but it's another leading question and it can't be done in re-examination. So I waive my objection to this leading question, but I don't want there to be leading questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I believe the witness has already answered that question because he said that nobody asked the witness about killings of civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the purpose of the question was whether he had the information. I will ask that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that question is also asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, then I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness heard of some killings later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you volunteer any information to the authorities about these killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. That one is vague beyond recognition, but in any event does not arise out of cross-examination. And therefore, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's out of the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, it appears I've run out of questions. That would be my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions? Yes, Judge El Mahdi, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I would seek some clarifications from you. The first thing is this: You answered a question by the Prosecution and you said that it would be unthinkable that the Croatian forces would shell or train their fire on their own citizens living in Croatian villages. If I quote you literally you said this: [In English] "It was unpredictable that HVO would result to using artillery against one of these -- of their own villages." [Interpretation] Are you really sure as to this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that the HVO shelled the area? I'm quite certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are. So were you there in person to see yourself firing from Croatian positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you can imagine the following situation. I was very close. Artillery fire can be heard sometimes at a distance of even tens or dozens of kilometres, and the distance I was from some shells that were falling was only several hundred metres. So yes, I was well able to assess and hear where a shell was being fired from and where it fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but were there not also ABiH positions beyond the Croatian positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were BH army soldiers in settlements -- in those settlements, but what I can say is that they were already mixed up with members of the HVO and the civilian population. So all of that was in one particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But are you sure that the firing was from Croatian positions and not from ABiH positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certain. I'm quite certain. The BH didn't have 2 per cent of the capacities that were used then in that area. So they couldn't -- nobody else could have used that, either the HVO or the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which were the weapons used then, according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, mortar weapons, the Howitzer was used, Howitzer artillery. There were attempts at using a tank. There was multiple-barrelled rocket launchers that were used, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and when -- when did the shelling start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 20 or 30 minutes after the beginning of the operation itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you properly, the action started around 5.30 or 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly thereabouts. At dawn, at daybreak. And then 20 or 30 minutes later artillery firing started and it went on for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But according to you, if there is a ground engagement can the artillery fire without the danger of hitting their own forces? Their own ground forces, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. However, we did not expect this, but that's what happened. And that's a fact. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how long do you think it lasted, this action, until 10.00, 11.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the action lasted until perhaps 1.00 p.m., perhaps a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean longer, so until around 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 3.00 or 4.00, but maybe up to 1.00, 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at 1.00 or 1.30, the ABiH forces withdrew. Is that what they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that you took part in a part of the attack. When did you do so? Where did you do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning I participated in a part of the attack on the left flank at a fortified position that was known as Borak and it is indicated on the photographs. After that, my group disbanded and I went back. I returned along an axis, or rather from the direction where there was danger that the HVO forces might cut across our communication lines, across a stream with the territory where our army was located. However, some of the soldiers were wounded and I took part of taking care of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore you only went up to Borak; you didn't go to Rajici or to Kriz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that there were large forces stationed in the Cer school amounting to how many people? How many fighters were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure, nobody counted them. But undoubtedly there was the largest number of them there and you can see that in the field with a naked eye. From our positions you could see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason why I'm asking you this is you said that the Croatian forces were spread and spent the nights in houses and not in the main building, which was the school building. So I guess that you meant that they were numerous enough?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What I had in mind is something quite different. In the school building the intervention units were accommodated, those who -- which could be deployed straight away. The units of the soldiers who were not active were not in the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they are the ones who would stay overnight in houses. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that those who were not on duty or not doing their shifts were. That is to say, they lived in their homes or at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move on to another subject. Regarding a document that was shown to you, it was a document addressed to the commander of the 6th Corps, a document drafted by Buza. It was said in the document that Croatian fighters were hiding and were even using human shields, civilians in other words. Sir, this document was shown to you; do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in the light -- in light of what you confirmed regarding lack of clarifications or -- in what Mr. Buza said to you, does it seem credible to you? Does this information seem credible to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely incorrect and unimaginable that the HVO should use its own civilians as a human shield. So I really don't know why he wrote that. The HVO used Bosniak civilians as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he used -- they used Bosnians. Did they use Bosnians? Were there Bosnians during their attack? Were there Bosnians living in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there weren't because Uzdol was an exclusively Croatian settlement; that's the first point. And secondly, the attack was prepared with the aim of having the surprise effect. So prisoners of war or military-abled Bosniaks or civilians could not have prepared beforehand. It was supposed to be a surprise attack, and I think that during the attack they weren't used nor were they there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, to my last question. It has to do with the involvement of the MUP in the attack. You told us that there were a few members of the MUP taking part in the attack. Were they under the orders of the commander, of the battalion commander, of the Prozor Independent Battalion that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were, and I think that it was considered a moral obligation on the part of policemen to take part in actions of this kind, so that as policemen there was a great pressure being exerted on them to take part, to participate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember when Mr. Halilovic came he addressed the soldiers. Were the MUP members there, too, when he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. And with respect to the number of soldiers, a number of MUP members -- well, there were very few of them, a negligible amount. I don't think there could have been more than five or six of them in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember what their mission was? Where were they supposed to intervene, in which area, in which village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript didn't record the last answer to Judge El Mahdi's last question as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was asking you where, in what area, village, the members of the MUP were taking part. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that at all. May I just add something? Within that entire action, more than 150 people took part, so I can't say where some four or five individuals were. I can't reconstruct it all now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but did not -- I think that every unit had its own mission or each group had their own mission. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think they had a separate group, that they made up a separate group. I think they were attached to some other groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, of course. I suppose that you remember in which group they were, where they operated. Do you remember that? You do, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, I think they've already been tendered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When we are adjourned, Madam Usher will pull down the blinds and she will show you out of this courtroom. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, you have something to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. It's just a couple of brief matters before the next witness starts. Your Honours, there's been some correspondence between the Prosecution and the Defence, in particular the Defence has sought answers to some questions. We received a reply to that from my learned friend Mr. Re, and we're considering the aspects of some of that so we're not going to raise the whole thing in front of the court. But there are a couple of matters that have to now be raised in court. The first one concerns a statement made by Sefer Halilovic to OTP investigators in 2001, which is an exhibit the Prosecution have on their 65 ter list and apparently intend to rely upon it and the Defence intend to challenge it if it's going to be relied upon. Your Honours, what we want to know now from the Prosecutor is through which witness is that document proposed to be tendered. We need an answer to that because there is no witness apparently left on the list who could conceivably be a relevant witness. So I invite the Prosecutor to tell us who it's going to come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's very easy. It's a recorded interview, a statement taken by Prosecution lawyer and Prosecution investigators in the presence of Halilovic's lawyers. In accordance with Rule 42 and 47 -- if I've got the correct Rules it's an admissible document and the Prosecution doesn't intend to call any witnesses to have the interview placed before the Trial Chamber because it's one which is -- there is a transcript. Everything that happened is recorded and it's a prime facie admissible. If the Trial Chamber wishes us to, we could call someone who was there at the time of the interview, but it's in our view a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The question is whether you are going to tender this document into the evidence or not; or if so, through which way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've just answered that. Yes, we are going to tender it; and we don't intend call a witness because it's -- that's Mr. Morrissey's question -- because it's an admissible statement of the accused taken in accordance with the rules. In my experience, the Prosecution doesn't normally call witnesses when tendering records of interview or statements made by an accused which are taken in accordance with the Rules before the Trial Chamber. The statement of itself is admissible if it's taken in accordance with the Rules. And there's nothing -- there's nothing on the face of it which would suggest it isn't. Why would we waste the Court's time by calling witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not encouraging you to call any witnesses. I just want to know -- you know, there are several ways to tender a document. For instance, the 92 bis, the live witnesses, and some other ways. So there must be a channel that you could use which is listed in our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We intend to tender it from the bar table as a -- the same as we would tender open source or legal documents. We would just tender it as a record of interview or statement made by the accused. We would tender it from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Any comments or objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We're going to object to that being tendered in any way, whether through a witness or through some other unusual practice. We certainly would object to it being tendered from the bar table, but we'll object to it whatever way it comes about. Your Honours, there are some nasty questions that the Defence would want to raise about this record of interview and how it was procured from Mr. Halilovic. So it's up to the Prosecutors how they want to proceed. But they've given us that information. The next question I have is: When is it proposed that they want to do that? Because we don't want to drop a -- we're going to move a motion that it not happen and we don't want to do that in a way that embarrasses the Chamber or is unfair to the Prosecutors. So if they tell us when they were proposing to do that, we'll advise of the schedule as to when we will allow you, the Tribunal, to rule on that matter. So that is the next question: When is it proposed to tender it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: During an appropriate break in the proceedings between witnesses. When we run out of witnesses, in my submission, is an appropriate time to do it. It will obviously take some argument, and it is when people are coming and going. We understand the Defence's position that they want to challenge it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, it is my first time to hear that there are going to be some documents introduced from the bar table. Would you please elaborate on these procedures so I could have some better understanding of this procedure, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. It's an admissible document in the Prosecution's submission; it's a taped interview between the accused and -- with his lawyer present and a Prosecution lawyer and a Prosecution investigator. It's an admissible document because it's a version the accused has given of what happened. It's a very lengthy document. There's -- it's been videotaped, audiotaped, and there's a very lengthy transcript of the statement. It's of itself admissible because it's a -- I mean, documents don't have to be tendered through witnesses. They can be tendered by consent. If it's a legal document from another country, for example, or something the Trial Chamber could take judicial notice of it, that would be tendered. Or a record of interview or statement falls into another category. That is, if it's prime facie within the Rules; taped; the accused has been cautioned, advised of his rights; has his lawyer present; and complies with the Rules, it is admissible under Rule 85 before the Trial Chamber. Now, if the Trial Chamber wants us to call someone who participated it to say, Yes, I was there, just like I am in the video, just like I am in the transcript, we could probably arrange to have someone come to court and say, Yes, we're all there and these are the questions that were asked and they appear in the video and the transcript. But our submission is that it is certainly something that complies with the Rules and on its face, in our submission it does, it is admissible as a document -- or the document being the transcript, the video and the audio is certainly admissible as a Prosecution exhibit to be tendered from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, do you have anything to say about this document tendered through the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that's a common-law practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's absolutely never been the common-law practice. The common-law practice is if someone interviews a suspect on video or on audio or any other form, they come along and attest to the accuracy of it and answer questions of how they procured it or how it was procured. And if there is an issue to be raised, it is raised through them. Your Honours haven't got an answer to the question you asked, and I haven't got an answer to the question that I asked. Your Honours, first of all, I want to know when the Prosecutor proposes to do it. It's not good enough to say between witnesses. This is an argument that'll take time and organising. The Prosecutor had better say when they it is that they propose to tender it. And then we'll see whether we're happy to do it then and the Chamber can indicate whether you're happy to do it then and we'll take it from there. So I'll ask for an answer to that question a second time. As to the issue Your Honour raised, as to the process, it's not the process here, from what I understand. My learned friend refers to foreign legal documents. They're irrelevant to this issue. Refers to matters that are by consent; that certainly isn't the case here. So there's no basis for doing it on the current face of things. However, the Prosecutors are entitled to consider that and they might think of a way in which it can be justified and put it in a motion and respond to our motion. And of course at that time they might have an argument to put, but I doubt it's going to be this one. Secondly, in the common-law system it would never happen and could never happen. I could indicate -- well, my experience doesn't matter. If the Court could benefit from research and learning on that, I will provide it to you. Because you've got to call a witness who procured the interview. All sorts of things happen in interviews and all sorts of things happen before they start. That's why a witness is called, to make sure that it's all bona fide and what you see is what you get. In this case, I don't want to make a speech about it now. We have a basis for challenging this and we're going to put it. It really is an important issue as to how the Prosecution proposes to proceed. We don't want them saying to the Tribunal, If you would like someone to be called. It's not up to you to decide these things; it's up to the Prosecutors. If the Prosecutors wish to amend their list of witnesses, then that's what they should do. Frankly, there was never a witness on the list that this Tribunal's had in front of it who could possibly have been the appropriate person for that interview. And it's not a question of things changing and them wanting to add someone now. It's just another one of the disasters facing the Prosecutor which we will point out when we come to do the motion. But Your Honours, it's not the time to do it now. I'm not seeking to run that argument now. We'll do it in the due course. What we want to know is when. And we think we're entitled to an answer on that topic, Your Honour. I would seek that the Prosecutor give us an answer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the time for our case is running out. We could not save this matter until the last minute. So I hope the Prosecution could make up their minds during this week and inform us about their intention and what kind of procedure they may apply in tendering those documents. You may make it as an oral submission or may file a written submission. Of course the Defence has the full right to make a response, but as I said before it should be done as early as possible, better before the 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, that's a sufficient indication for us. The Prosecution can tell us sometime this week and that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours, I've got other matters to raise. I notice there's a witness there and I can deal with this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just ask one thing. My learned friend Mr. Weiner indicated the likelihood or possibility of some Rule 89 (F) procedures to shorten things. As I have indicated before, we're happy to cooperate with that if they tell us they've got people in that category. We haven't been told of any yet. But Mr. Weiner, I have been told, has been tied up, and that's understandable. We're open to being approached by the Prosecutors to tell us who they want to use that procedure with, and we can talk to them about it. But we just need to know in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is our position that we will encourage both parties to apply the Rule 89 (F), and if so I believe the other party should be informed as early as possible. Yes, could we have the next witness, please, since he has been waiting here at least for the whole afternoon and we only have 45 minutes to go for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Stojanovic. Your name is Janjko Stojanovic and you were born on 8 November 1970. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were born in Uzdol and your occupation is deputy foreman of construction?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your mother is Ivka Stojanovic, who testified here last week?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You lived in Uzdol until April 1994?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in September 1993 you were a serving member of the HVO. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I think in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your service in the HVO mainly in the area you lived, that is in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that the HVO had a base in the school in Cer. What was in that -- what was in that base?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. People.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about communications?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The main communications centre was somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think personal weapons. Each man had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there facilities to feed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the to accommodate them?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know how many it could accommodate in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many. Up to 20 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many, to your knowledge, HVO soldiers were there stationed in the Uzdol area as of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: An approximate number?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 80 and 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how many positions did the HVO have around Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: About ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How were they manned?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean each of the positions, or the total of the ten positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The ten positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think the witness is entitled to have that one clarified. When my friend -- the witness asked to know whether or not he's being asked about each of the positions or the total, and my learned friend then said "the ten positions," which leaves him in the same position he was in before. So it ought to be clarified which of the two alternatives put by the witness he's being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to me it's clear. But for the sake of the record, Mr. Re, would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what I want you to tell the Trial Chamber is: How were those positioned manned? What did the HVO do to ensure that there were soldiers in them? How did it work? Were there shifts, for example?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did that work?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Three shifts. Some walked and some used the lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did each of those positions have a similar number of soldiers in them on those three shifts or did it vary?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the positions you occupied? Which ones were they?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were just two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were your positions? Which ones did you go to?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Borak and Komin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying there were only two soldiers in each of these positions?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many soldiers did you go into these positions with, firstly in Borak?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Five, six.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did the shifts go for?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was in -- what comprised the position at Borak?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe the position. What was there?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers, trenches, and a wooden hut in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What weaponry did you have to defend the position?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kalashnikov rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were those -- were Kalashnikovs issued to all the HVO soldiers in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just go back to the -- we'll just stay with the position at the moment. Were there any fixed weaponry in that particular position at Borak?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: PKT, a weapon called Zbrojovka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you explain what kind of weapon that is in lay terms for the Tribunal, what sort of weapon it is.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's very much like a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any heavier weapons at that position such as mortars?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of mortars were they and how many did you have?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 160-millimetre, but it wasn't always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just go back to the Kalashnikov rifles. You said a moment ago that they weren't issued to all the HVO soldiers in Uzdol. Who were the HVO soldiers in Uzdol armed with?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Some had semi-automatic rifles, some had snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your weapon?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you issued with hand grenades? That's you personally.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the soldiers in your position, in Borak, did they have hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, at least none were visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the rocket-propelled grenades, did you, that is the soldiers in Uzdol, have rocket-propelled grenades?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please try to be more specific. You mean heavy ones or light ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The light ones, the shoulder-fire ones.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The light ones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The heavier ones?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the multiple-rocket launchers, did you have any of those?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the HVO have a Howitzer in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the armoured personnel carriers, did they have any of those?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tanks?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was one from time to time near the base, but I never heard it firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it was there on the 14th of September? That was when the attack occurred.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that the tank was there from time to time. Do you know where it went when it wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it went to Prozor, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often was it there? What percentage of the time was it there? If you could cast your mind back.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not much of the time. Over a year, can I use that as a yardstick, or do you want some sort of a monthly average?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, but whichever you can.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was only ever around when there was the danger of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how often was that?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Several days. Three to five, say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any rank when you were in the HVO in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the other soldiers who were with you in the trench on Borak?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a shift commander when you were on duty in Borak?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the communications -- I'm sorry. What form of communication did you use between your position on Borak and the base at the school?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The field telephone, it had a wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a radio?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the beginning. But later, yes, we had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the preference, radio or field telephone?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Field telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe your uniform.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the patterned kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Patterned, does that mean camouflage?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the headgear?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing for the most part. A bandanna here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did all the soldiers -- sorry, the HVO soldiers in Uzdol wear the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think most did, but some had their own uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you wear any badges or insignia of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did others?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the HVO uniform in Uzdol different to that of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did it differ?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was more the colour of sand and the chequers were a bit smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On which one?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which was more the colour of sand with smaller chequers, the ABiH or the HVO uniform?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim uniform, the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you living in Uzdol in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you a full-time soldier?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you going between your shifts and home?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about your mother, Ivka? Was she coming to stay with you sometimes?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just to see how I was doing. She would do some washing. She would cook something for me, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a grandmother who also lived in the area?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was her name and where did she live?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lucija Zelenika, and she resided in Zelenike.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about the days just before the attack on Uzdol by the ABiH. Were your mother and grandmother in the village in the days before the attack?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify, because my grandmother was in a different village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When I say "village," I meant the Uzdol -- the hamlets comprising Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were they and how did they get there?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I drove them over from the village of Rumboc in a car. I took my grandmother to Zelenike and I took my mother back to her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you take your grandmother to Zelenike?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: She insisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you take her to her house in Zelenike?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long was that before the attack?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Three to five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you want your mother to come with you to your house?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Because she would have been alone while I was away on shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was afraid that someone would attack her while I was not around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the someone you were afraid might attack her?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim forces. There was danger nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you in the two days before the attack?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. What do you mean two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The day before and the day before that. Were you the front line, in your position, at your home, or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was working my shift, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you spend the nights?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any other soldiers spend those nights at home with you, or was it just you and your mother?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Alone with my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And on the day before the attack were you -- I withdraw that. About what time did you come back?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean on that day or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 13th.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was free on the 13th, on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you and your mother do that night? That's the night of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The night of the 13th, you're talking about the day before the attack, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. What did you do that night before you went to bed?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th I was on the day shift, daytime shift. The night of the 13th I spent sleeping, as usual. And my next shift was supposed to be the night of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before we come to what happened on the 14th, I want to show you some photographs and to have you assist the Trial Chamber by marking some things on, specifically HVO and ABiH positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please -- could we please have on the screen photograph number 0299-2289.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 342.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stojanovic, can you recognise that as a photo -- an overhead photograph taken from behind the village of Here?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the hill called Borak there?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you see the village of Kriz where your parents' house was or is?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could assist us by -- can you circle the village -- can you circle Kriz for us.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just write "Kriz" above it, please.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you see your -- where your position on Borak is? That's the HVO position. Can you see that in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you mark it with a straight line.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just write "HVO Borak" above that.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see to the -- just to the right above where you've written Kriz there's a hill there. What's that hill called?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any ABiH positions on that hill?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you be able to mark those in with a line, please.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just write "ABiH" above that, please.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any ABiH positions underneath where you have written HVO?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you mark those in, please.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not quite clear, but it should be around about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what that area was called?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was between the village of Here and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you also please write "ABiH" under that so it's clear to us that's an ABiH position.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the -- thank you. And what is the distance between -- the approximate distance between your position on Borak and the ABiH position just below Here in metres?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From where your position was, could you see the ABiH position?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you see it with the naked eye or did you need binoculars or some other assistance?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the from the village of Kriz? Could you see the ABiH position in Here from there?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not from everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P343.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 0299-2300.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the hill at the bottom middle of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that Borak?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see there where your positions, that's the HVO positions, were?

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please mark those in. Draw them in with a line.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And please just put HVO above that.

utterances.speaker: JANJKO STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
